passages.t: ‘We have sinned like our fathers’: the same story, told as confession
passages.happening:
Psalm 106 is the second of the pair. Psalm 105 told the story of God's faithfulness. Psalm 106 tells the same story as a confession.

It begins with praise. “Hallelujah! Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever” (verse 1). The singer asks God to remember him too (verse 4).

Then the turn. “We have sinned like our fathers; we have done wrong and acted wickedly” (verse 6). The singer does not say ‘they’. He says ‘we’.

Then the story. In Egypt they did not understand God's wonders, and “they rebelled by the sea” (verse 7). “Yet He saved them for the sake of His name” (verse 8). He dried up the Red Sea (verse 9). They believed and sang (verse 12). “Yet they soon forgot His works” (verse 13).

They craved food in the desert (verse 14). They were jealous of Moses and Aaron (verse 16). “At Horeb they made a calf and worshiped a molten image” (verse 19). “They exchanged their Glory for the image of a grass-eating ox” (verse 20). God would have destroyed them, “had not Moses His chosen one stood before Him in the breach to divert His wrath from destroying them” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Praying the sins of your people, and not only your own, was a known form of prayer in Israel, especially after the exile. Ezra 9, Nehemiah 9 and Daniel 9 hold long prayers like it. Daniel prays, “we have sinned and done wrong. We have acted wickedly and rebelled” (Daniel 9:5).

This is Israel's own honest confession, spoken by Israel to God. That matters. A people that tells its own history this way is not proud. It is humble before God. The story it tells could be told of any people, and of the church too.

‘Exchanged their Glory’ (verse 20) is a sharp phrase. Their ‘Glory’ was God himself. They traded him for a metal ox that eats grass.

To stand ‘in the breach’ (verse 23) is a picture from war. When a city wall was broken, a soldier stood in the gap to hold off the enemy. Moses stood in the gap between the people and God's anger, and prayed.
passages.later:
Paul echoes verse 20 when he writes that people “exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal man and birds and animals and reptiles” (Romans 1:23). He also says, “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).

Paul tells the church that the wilderness stories “took place as examples to keep us from craving evil things as they did” (1 Corinthians 10:6). The warning is for Christians.
passages.asks:
Can you say ‘we’ about sin, as this psalm does? It is easy to blame the people before us, or the people beside us. Psalm 106 teaches a harder and more honest prayer: we have sinned like our fathers.

And notice Moses in verse 23. Is there someone you can stand ‘in the breach’ for, praying for them when they are in danger?

passages.t: ‘Nevertheless He heard their cry’, and Book Four ends
passages.happening:
The confession goes on. They refused the good land and would not believe (verse 24). They grumbled in their tents (verse 25). They joined in the worship of Baal of Peor (verse 28), and a plague broke out until Phinehas stepped in (verses 29 to 30). At Meribah they angered God, and Moses spoke rashly (verses 32 to 33).

In the land they did worse. They took up the customs of the nations around them (verse 35). “They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons” (verse 37). So God gave them over to their enemies (verses 40 to 42). “Many times He rescued them, but they were bent on rebellion and sank down in their iniquity” (verse 43).

Then the great word of the psalm. “Nevertheless He heard their cry; He took note of their distress” (verse 44). “And He remembered His covenant with them, and relented by the abundance of His loving devotion” (verse 45).

The singer prays: “Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from the nations” (verse 47). And then Book Four ends with its blessing. “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. Let all the people say, ‘Amen!’ Hallelujah!” (verse 48).
passages.hearers:
‘Gather us from the nations’ (verse 47) shows who first prayed this psalm: people scattered in exile after Babylon took Jerusalem, or people back home waiting for the rest to return. They told the old story to understand their own disaster, and they found in it the same God who kept hearing his people's cry.

Child sacrifice (verses 37 to 38) was practised by some peoples around Israel. The law of Moses forbade it (Deuteronomy 12:31), and the history books record with horror that some kings of Judah did it (2 Kings 21:6). The psalm calls it what it is: innocent blood.

Verse 48 is the doxology that closes Book Four, as the book page explains, matching the blessings at the end of Books One, Two and Three (41:13; 72:18-19; 89:52). Verses 1 and 47 to 48 also close the song in 1 Chronicles 16, where “all the people said, ‘Amen!’” (1 Chronicles 16:36).
passages.later:
Paul asks, “did God reject His people? Certainly not” (Romans 11:1). He writes, “For God's gifts and His call are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). Psalm 106's ‘Nevertheless’ runs all the way into the New Testament.

John writes, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
passages.hard:
Two verses here are hard. Verse 34 blames Israel for not destroying the peoples of Canaan, and verses 30 to 31 praise Phinehas, who killed a man and a woman at Peor (Numbers 25:7-8). Christians read the conquest texts in several ways: as a one-time judgment in that ancient time and place, not a pattern for any later people; as the strong language of war common in ancient records; or by noting that the Old Testament itself shows Canaanite people surviving and joining Israel. Christians agree that the New Testament turns the fight against idols to the heart and the church, not the sword. The psalm's own concern is worship. Israel ‘adopted their customs’ and ended by sacrificing its children. No reading of these verses gives anyone today any right to harm another person or people.

This psalm is Israel's confession, in Israel's own voice. It gives no one any ground to blame or look down on the Jewish people. Christians who read it should hear their own story in it, and say ‘we’.
passages.asks:
Psalm 106 tells a long story of failure, and the word that saves it is ‘Nevertheless’ (verse 44). God heard. God remembered. God relented.

Has your story been one of the same failures, again and again? Psalm 106 does not ask you to pretend otherwise. It asks you to confess it, and to trust the God who still hears. Then say with the whole people, at the end of Book Four, ‘Amen’.
